chapter_theme: Paripadal 13 and 14: Nallezhuthiyar's hymn to Thirumal, the god as mountain, as the five senses and the elements, as the reclining one, the plough-bearer and the boar, counted down through five, four, three, two and one; and Kesavanar's hymn to Sevvel, his hill in the rains and a litany of his delights; both close by calling the god mother and asking only for more worship.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of Thirumal's form and ornaments: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

paripadal:13:1-13.reading: The poet hails Maal, whose flowered cloth has the beauty of the sun riding over a cloud-capped gem hill, whose garland vies in colour with a waterfall of gold and gems, whose banner bears the bird and whose discus has the cool grace of the wide moon; the discus and conch in his hands are like the two different discs that adorn the sky in their season, and his holy chest, with gold ornaments flashing like lightning and a garland shaped like a waterfall, holds by right for those who worship it the heaven that is theirs.
paripadal:13:1-13.nuance: The whole unit is a single figure of the god as a mountain: the cloth is the sun on the peak, the garland the waterfall, the ornaments the lightning, the discus and conch the sun and moon. The last clause turns the description to its use: the chest is not only beautiful but is where worshippers' heaven lies (உரிது அமர் துறக்கமும் உரிமை நன்கு உடைத்து).

comparisons.tenor: the beauty of the god's flowered cloth
the discus and conch held in the god's hands
the pearl garland on the chest

thinai_evidence.note: the god named as the senses and the elements, praise under paadaan

paripadal:13:14-21.reading: Taste, sound, sight, smell and touch are you, lord of killing war, and so are the faculties that take each of them; of the five just named, the sky praised as known by one is you, the wind known by two is you, the fire known by three is you, and the water known by four is you.
paripadal:13:14-21.nuance: The count is cumulative: each element is known through one more of the five than the one before (sky by sound, wind by sound and touch, and so on), so the list is a small theory of the elements, not a catalogue. The earth, which would be known by all five, is not named; the unit stops at water and line 22 turns with அதனால் to the worlds, so either the earth is left for the hearer to supply or the poet means the whole of what follows to stand for it.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the one god who became three forms, under paadaan

paripadal:13:22-36.reading: Therefore the thrice-seven worlds, the root, aram, time that passed beyond all firstness, the sky, and the wind with the fire are of your side; and you are the one who, divided, became three forms: the one wearing tulasi who lies in waking sleep on the bed of the serpent with forked tongues and a thousand spread hoods flashing with gems, in the midst of the milk sea; the one of the curved plough who ploughs into the chests of those who come against him beyond measure with a roaring army, raising dust as he digs; and the tusker with the bright shining tusk that planted the whole root so that the four lands should not shake.
paripadal:13:22-36.nuance: The three forms are the reclining Maal, the plough-bearer and the boar who raised the earth; the poem makes the plough-bearer, elsewhere Maal's elder brother, a form of Maal himself (மூஉரு ஆகிய தலைபிரி ஒருவனை). களிறு usually means an elephant, but the tusk that props the earth points to the boar. Whose form the milk sea rivals in line 25 (தன் உரு உறழும்) is unclear: the white serpent's seems likelier than the dark god's. The syntax of lines 22 to 24 is loose, and the reading of நின் மருங்கின்று as 'at your side, from you' is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's banner, body, grace and feet, under paadaan

paripadal:13:37-48.reading: The poet hails the unswerving rich one who took as banner the many-coloured, wide-winged enemy of snakes, lord of the high bird banner whom good praises name in the sweet ancient word of command; his beautiful body rivals five things, the rain cloud, the kaaya flower, the sea, darkness and the sapphire, and four things, the right-whorled conch, the pouring cloud, the rumbling sky and the roaring thunderbolt, rival his grace, his wrath and his words; the shade of his anklet lies past what is finished, what is passing and what is still budding; those who praise it are without the two deeds, and his heart holds to a single deed.
paripadal:13:37-48.nuance: The poet counts his comparisons aloud (அவை ஐந்தும், அவை நான்கும், அவை மூன்றும்), so the unit is built as a falling series five, four, three, two, one: five dark things for the body, four sounds for grace, wrath and speech, three times surpassed by the feet, two deeds absent, one deed in his heart. Line 47 can be read either way: the praisers have no twofold karma, or the god's feet that they praise have none. How the four sounds are shared out among arul, seral and vayin mozhi is not certain.

comparisons.vehicle: கார், மலர்ப் பூவை, கடலை, இருள், மணி
வலம்புரி, வாய்பொழி, அதிர்பு வான், முழக்குச் செல்
comparisons.tenor: the god's grace, wrath and words

thinai_evidence.note: the closing prayer of a hymn to Maal, under paadaan

paripadal:13:49-63.reading: Feet, hands, eyes and mouth are lotuses opened past their sheath; you are great in feet, shoulders and neck, wide in chest, hips and mind, subtle in learning, knowledge and aram, ardent in sacrifice, valour and desire, of unfailing strength and red eyes that do not rage, rich lord of the war-winning discus, whose chest loves the fragrant twisted tulasi garland set with fire-bright flowers; thinking of you as our mother we have worshipped your feet, bowed many times and praised you, by the fruit of the penance we did before and before; still more and still more, this is our desire.
paripadal:13:49-63.nuance: The last line uses காமம், the word for erotic longing, for the wish to worship: what the devotees desire is not a gift but more of this same worship, which they treat as the fruit of past penance. The god is thought of as mother (அன்னை எனநினைஇ), not father or king. The catalogue groups the body by threes and fours with a quality for each group (பெரியை, பரியை, நுண்ணியை, வெய்யை).

comparisons.tenor: the god's feet, hands, eyes and mouth

thinai_evidence.note: the god's hill in the rains, praised as his: paadaan

paripadal:14:1-18.reading: The heavy rain has poured, the brimming pools are in flower; the hum of the bright bees sipping the pollen of the cool kadamba is like a band of musicians; the shoulders of the women who dwell at your feet as they dance are like the bamboo on the high slopes; the full cry of the peacock with its crest like the bright vaakai flower is like the words of those who tell lovers who joined and left, 'do not delay, come'; the fresh konrai is like a golden garland; the vengai's blossoms have spread over the broad rock so that it shows the women in tears a tiger; and along the kaanthal by the water and the soft thonri on its creepers, flowers hot as coral have spread: your hill is full of the rains, you of the shining weapon who cut down Sur in battle.
paripadal:14:1-18.nuance: The peacock simile carries the akam convention of the rains as the season the absent lover promised to return by: on the god's hill the peacock's cry is heard as the very summons 'do not delay, come', so a love situation sits inside the praise without a speaker of its own. Line 12 is hard: it may mean that the flower-strewn rock looks like a tiger to the weeping women, or that it reports a tiger to them; the sense of அழுகை மகளிர் is not fixed.

comparisons.tenor: the hum of the bees at the kadamba
the vengai blossoms spread on the rock

thinai_evidence.note: a litany of the god's delights ending in the prayer, under paadaan

paripadal:14:19-32.reading: The poet hails the god who delights in the fragrant smoke of naRai rising like a spotless dark rain cloud, who with six faces and twelve shoulders won and loved the fragrant-flowered Valli, who delights in the song his kin raise as they gather round him, whose glory on the day he was born made the great ones fear him, and who delights in the aram of the brahmins, twice-born, of two names, of moist heart and one name; since you are our mother, the fruit of our worshipping you again and again, close by you, let it be these same things more and more, more even than the many of your fame of ancient ripened tradition.
paripadal:14:19-32.nuance: The four delights the litany names are offerings and worship (the smoke, the song, the brahmins' aram) with the love of Valli set among them, so the god's love-match is counted as one of the things worship gives him. The prayer asks that the fruit of worship be அவை, 'those', most naturally the same acts again, as Paripadal 13 asks. The brahmins' string in lines 27 and 28 (இரு பிறப்பு, இரு பெயர், ... ஒரு பெயர்) is a riddle of counts whose exact referents (the two names, the one name) are not certain.

links.note: Both name the same five, taste, light or sight, touch, sound and smell; the Kural, in its chapter on renunciants, puts the world in the grasp of the one who discerns them, while Paripadal 13 says the five and the faculties that take them are the god.
links.teaches: The Kural's five, which the renunciant must master, are in the Paripadal the god himself, so the same old list of five could ground either a discipline of withdrawal from the senses or a worship through them.

links.note: Paripadal 13 orders the elements sky, wind, fire, water by how many of the five each is known through; Tirumanthiram 385 tells the same chain as emergence, space, air, then a doubtful கான், water, the five together.
links.teaches: Because the Paripadal's count puts fire between wind and water, it supports reading the Tirumanthiram's obscure கான் as fire, and shows the creation chain the later Saiva text tells already present in an early Tamil hymn as a theory of how each element is known.

links.note: Paripadal 2 says Maal is younger to those who call him the white one's younger brother and elder to those who call him elder; Paripadal 13 makes the plough-bearer one of Maal's own three forms.
links.teaches: Held together, the two hymns show Paripadal poets resolving the kinship of Maal and the plough-bearer in two ways: one makes the order of birth depend on who is speaking, the other dissolves the kinship entirely by making the brother a form of the one god.

links.note: Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; Paripadal 13 line 47 says the two deeds are absent where his feet are praised, and gives the god a heart set on a single deed.
links.teaches: The Paripadal sets the Kural's claim inside a theology: the praisers are free of both deeds because the god himself is beyond the three times and holds to one deed, so the Kural's freedom from karma through praise is grounded in what the praised one is.

links.note: Two hymns by different poets to different gods, Nallezhuthiyar's to Maal and Kesavanar's to Sevvel, close the same way: the god thought of as mother, worship repeated, and இன்னும் இன்னும் asking for more of it.
links.teaches: Since the same close serves two poets and both Maal and Murugan, the mother-address and the prayer for more worship belong to a shared Paripadal liturgy, not to one poet's devotion or one god's cult.

links.note: Paripadal 5 refuses wealth, gold and pleasure and asks the god for grace, love and aram; Paripadal 13 asks for nothing but more of the worship, which it calls the fruit of past penance and names its kaamam.
links.teaches: Read in sequence the two closes show a step in the hymns' idea of what to ask: from the god's virtues instead of wealth to worship as its own reward, so that by Paripadal 13 the act of praising is both the fruit of tapas and the whole of desire.

links.note: In Akananuru 194 the heroine hears the peacock cry in the very rains her lover named for his return and he has not come; in Paripadal 14 the peacock's cry on the god's rainy hill is like the words calling the departed lover 'do not delay, come'.
links.teaches: The Paripadal's simile only works for a hearer who knows the mullai convention the Akananuru poem dramatises, the rains as the deadline of return, so the devotional poet borrows the heroine's grief as an ornament of the god's hill and makes the peacock say the summons she can only feel.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai describes the twice-born at Eragam in full, never failing in the six duties, keeping the three fires and chanting at the proper hour; Paripadal 14 compresses them to a riddle of counts, இரு பிறப்பு, இரு பெயர், ஒரு பெயர், and says the god delights in their aram.
links.teaches: The idyll's full portrait supplies what the Paripadal's terse count assumes, so its இரு பிறப்பு is the same இருபிறப்பாளர் the idyll names, and the brahmins' ritual life is shown to be, for both poems, one of the things Murugan is praised for enjoying.

source_issues: Paripadal 13: the source's printed line numbers drift; the number 25 stands on our line 24, and the song has 63 lines while the source numbers its last line 64. Line numbers here are the ones show prints.
Paripadal 13 line 59: துழா அய் is printed as two words (the lengthened துழாய்); the karu form is taken as துழா.
